utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is the Defence ready to continue the re-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness, Mr. Gray, into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gray.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least the weather did not oppose against having a nice weekend. I hope you had. Mr. Gray, may I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your re-examination will be continued. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Re-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Gray.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just bear with me for a few seconds? I'm referring to your testimony of last Friday. Unfortunately, I can't refer to the page. Do you remember that you were asked a certain number of questions concerning the arrival of Mr. Douglas Hurd's convoy in the city of Sarajevo and in particular, with regard to the problems of the elevations from which the Serbs allegedly shelled? What you wanted to say at around 10.00 was something to do with what we call the primary in English, the Prosecution interrupted you and said that they would return to that subject, they never did so. What did you want to say exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please put a question to the witness. There's no need to comment on the behaviour of the other party while questioning the witness, if that is what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's a second objection. You may recall, Mr. President that on Friday in re-examination, Mr. Piletta-Zanin sought to bring out in cross-examination this issue of the primaries which was not a topic of cross-examination and I think, Mr. President, you ruled that if Mr. Piletta-Zanin asked questions in relation to that issue, then further cross-examination would be allowed so I don't know whether this question is asked on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, I didn't make any kind of comment. All I did was indicate what happened so that memory of the witness could be refreshed after an absence of 48 hours and secondly, when the witness wanted to say something and when he wants to be explicit it's necessary that he should do so. The Prosecution said that they would return to that subject, they didn't, otherwise we would have made the objection before, but I will leave the matter to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the matter does not result from cross-examination, you are not entitled to do that. But I will ask Mr. Gray. When you told us about the primary, what would you like to add? What did you have in mind to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. When I was standing at the very front entrance to the Presidency building, I clearly heard -- and I have taken courses and -- in mortars. I clearly heard the primary of a mortar going off, a very short way from where the actual impacts took place. A primary is a -- it's exactly that, I mean, it is like a shotgun cartridge in the bottom of the tail fin of a mortar bomb and then you have around it other charges to actually make the mortar go further. I clearly heard the primaries of these mortar bombs and they were very, very close and they were very clearly directed at a particular target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could hear that they were directed to a particular target; is that what you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm saying that they were so close that you could hear -- you could actually hear the primary go off and then the bomb would land a few seconds later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would be the distance, approximately, if you -- are you talking about 10 metres, 50 metres, 100 metres, 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, a primary would be -- a maximum distance for a primary is 200 metres, that's it. End of story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at what distance did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard it at approximately 50 metres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in what direction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It came -- if you have the Presidency building there, and the front doors are there, and you have the main street here, then they came from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I take it that since you're using your left arm that -- if you are standing in front of the building that you are pointing in the westerly direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see anything apart from hearing the primary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw them land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know, but firing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't actually see them, but they were just down a street to the left of the Presidency building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes and you say a couple of seconds later, after you heard that, you tell us three, four, five, six?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, mortar bombs go straight up and they come straight down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes I'm not asking for -- I'm asking you for the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe five, six seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five, six seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do understand your answer that apart from hearing it and seeing them landing that you didn't saw them being fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to the same subject, at about 10.25, you answered a question put to you by the Prosecution. You were asked how do you know that the shell couldn't have and we're talking about the market, couldn't have hit a person, couldn't have fallen on a person? My question is as follows: If a shell hit a person, could it have left traces on the ground which would be similar to the ones that you found at this market near the PTT building? Have you under the question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have. There would be -- when a mortar bomb goes off, I mean it -- sorry, it explodes, irrespective of whether or not it hits a person or it hits the ground, only the actual bomb, the explosive part actually explodes. The tail fin is always left quite separately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gray, my question was -- my question, Colonel, was whether the crater that you found at the market could have been caused by a shell that exploded after hitting the head or the shoulder of someone who was there or perhaps this is not possible?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is totally impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now interested in this ambush, the ambush of the UN convoy which came under fire from Butmir, we spoke about this at about 10.30, you remember the video. They mentioned fighting that had been going on for days and you said that you had negotiated a cease-fire. My question is do you remember who you negotiated the cease-fire with and do you remember what the purpose of the cease-fire was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I negotiated the cease-fire with both sides, specifically to bring the convoy in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you there, thank you. Once you had negotiated this cease-fire with the two sides, when you negotiated, did they indicate any hours, did they say that it would be in force from a certain hour in the morning to a certain hour in the afternoon, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We negotiated the cease-fire in order to bring the convoy in at a specific time. From my memory, it was 10.00 in the morning. The convoy had been sitting at Lukavica barracks overnight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you said that in your opinion, that fire was only coming from the Presidency side. My question is: Do you know whether the enemy side responded and if so, what was targeted in this response?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fire came from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object on the basis that the witness has not been asked to distinguish between what he saw firsthand and what information came to him from other sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah, would you please specify your question in such a way that we know what's the basis of the knowledge on which the witness answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I will be glad to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you are able to answer this question, could you tell us what information you have about this subject? Can you tell us what the origin, the source of your knowledge is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fire came from Butmir, it was very clearly from one side. It did not come from the Serb side. The Presidency side had a camera crew there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I apologise. I will stop you there. My question is: How did you know this? Because I don't think you were in the convoy itself so what is the source of your information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interviewed and I had extensive questioning after the event about the presence of camera crews at the actual location, I have --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who asked you these questions, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came from UNPROFOR headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a written report which was compiled after this incident and which was submitted to the authorities; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'll go back to the question. According to information that you had at the time, do you know whether the Serbian forces responded to the fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, how do you know, Mr. Gray, because that was the issue? How did you know that they did not respond, not being there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I spoke to the people who actually -- the people that were involved in the incident because fire was only coming from one direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean the people involved in the incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The French soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I thought that I was quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... In which he said that he was interviewed and that it was not that clear and it was not specifically on the response. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to the issue of Lukavica. This was at about 11:21. You were asked questions about the targets in Lukavica, whether they were legitimate or not and then you were asked about windows in Lukavica, you were asked details about the windows in Lukavica; do you remember these questions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is do you know whether some windows in the Lukavica barracks were protected in a certain manner and if they were, how were they protected, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The windows were not protected and a number of them -- I mean, we had one meeting where I signed an agreement with Professor Koljevic and we had to have the meeting in the corridor of the building because we were receiving so much -- I mean the building was physically shaking and the shrapnel was coming through the windows at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, at 12.06 I would like you to expand on what you said. You said that you usually met General Galic when it was necessary to establish a cease-fire. My question is with regard to concluding a cease-fire, what was General Galic's attitude to cease-fires; was he against it, was he in favour of it, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was most cooperative. I mean he was in favour of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How can you affirm this before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- I mean, he enabled me to have a guided tour of all of the weapons that were not under or currently under UN supervision. I mean, he was most cooperative in doing all of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to this subject, the Prosecution asked you a question which was: How do you know that they showed you all their heavy weapons? My question in relation to this matter is: Could you have discovered these heavy weapons that you weren't aware of at the time if the Serbian forces hadn't spontaneously pointed them out to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had observers in a number of positions. I established beyond the first five positions that we had for the Serbian side, we established another two positions. This was in spite of the fact that I had lost a number of observers because they had been wounded and we were aware, beyond the ones that were agreed -- I mean they showed us, I mean they agreed to show us these extra positions. We were aware that there were a number of other ones but they were very, very small and -- I mean we were aware of where the firing was coming from. We knew that. We could see it. We can hear it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, in relation to the issue of the PTT building, you said that the building consisted of three basements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony, and on the tape that we saw, we had the impression that there was a higher level with a window and I'd like you to explain to us briefly something about how the land lies there because normally in cellars, in basements, there are no windows.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The PTT was built up on a level. In order to actually enter the front entrance of the PTT, you had to drive up a ramp on to a parking level and that explains the three levels that were actually below it because the levels went down and the front entrance was raised up. I wish I had brought photos to actually explain this but they are on the videotapes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, am I to understand that the building is on a slope which allows different levels on different sides of the building?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building was -- the subbasement levels were deliberately built and the workshop level was obviously one of them, but they also had a parking area under there as well. But the ramp that you can see in one of the videos that I provided goes up and then you have the main building which goes up for five storeys, there is another part of the building which goes up for three storeys, but underneath the building, there are three storeys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Colonel, you told us that Holiday Inn was also used by snipers and hence my question: How do you know that? How did they hide there and what did they use for this, what do you know about that? And what did they target; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They targeted human beings --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have time to check the transcripts thoroughly but my recollection is that the manner in which the Holiday Inn came up was the witness' attention was drawn to a building which he'd earlier seen on the video and at first he thought I was referring to the Holiday Inn, his attention was then directed to what we know to be the parliament building. If that's the case, if that's the reference my learned colleague is referring to, then because it arose on the basis of a misunderstanding by the witness, in my respectful submission, that's not a proper topic for cross-examination because I then, having directed the witness to the appropriate building, did not pursue it, his misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace. -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, to save time which is available, let us move on to another issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, with regard to that tape that the Prosecution mentioned, one could see people reacting after an attack and my question is as follows: If the purpose -- if the attack is performed with incendiaries and its purpose is to destroy with fire, what is usually called a sniper nest, according to your military experience, wouldn't have been legitimate to stop the enemy side to try to protect its sniper nest from such fire, that is, by distinguishing the fire?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, correction. By extinguishing the fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the translation, it is said by distinguishing the fire and I do understand that it's extinguishing the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, you can see it on the screen, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you understand the question or shall I rephrase it? If I want to destroy a sniper nest, and if the enemy side wishes to protect it by extinguishing the fire as a result of an incendiary bullet, is it possible to prevent that? Is it possible to do something to prevent that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fire that happened against the building that we saw in the videotape, as far as I understand, came from the Presidency side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, sorry, I'm asking you a question which is based on your technical knowledge. Try, please, to follow me. If a side, whichever, destroys a sniper nest by using incendiaries and if the other side wishes to protect or to preserve this nest by extinguishing the fire, is it possible to prevent such a firefighter's action by further action, by further fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I return to another question. The Ukranian Battalion, you were asked in relation to the commentary, again on a story and you were asked if you realised that it was incoming fire at that point or rather a little bit before that, before you did not wait for the end of the question, but within the same context, you wanted to draw attention to the barracks in relation to the topography, to the exact locations, what can you -- what was it that you wanted to tell us and what was that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ukranians were based in Marsal Tito barracks and it was a very unfortunate position for the Ukranian Battalion. They were immediately targeted not by the Serbs, but they were targeted by the Presidency forces and I go back to what I said before, the UN selection of battalions to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, sorry, no, no, I'm sorry but I have to interrupt you. But what we want to know is the topography. Why did you want to speak to us about the location of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barracks are important because they are in the very centre of Sarajevo and the location is very important because the -- the Serbs had very little visibility of the actual barracks themselves. They were totally blinded from the east and the west and the north and the only place they could actually see them was from the south.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean that there was no direct visibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only from the south. Only from the south.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, there were -- there was talk about night attacks and you were asked if you heard comments which spoke about reprisals, so my question is as follows: Is it legitimate, militarily, if an attack is launched at night to endeavour to stop it by gunfire? Be it mortar or artillery fire which happens at night and in order to establish exactly -- in view of the forces which are confronting you and which are involved in this attack?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is legitimate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'd like us now to focus on what the Prosecution called your theories regarding Muslims. In one of the questions -- one of his questions, the Prosecutor clearly indicated that you had some theories concerning the Muslims. When you used the term "Muslims," within a particular context of the Sarajevo war, in which sense did you use it; can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used it in the sense that the Muslims were the predominant element in the military factions who were fighting the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Presidency side, the so-called Presidency side, was it or not usually called that, that is, the Muslim party or the Muslims during your tour of duty in Sarajevo; is that how they were referred to usually?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were normally referred to as the Presidency. That's why we had the Papa side which was Presidency and then we had the Lima side which was the Serb side and the Lima side was purely based on the fact that the headquarters was based at Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Do you have any theory for or against the Muslims; in other words, would you have a theory which would be racist or not for or against the Muslims? Do you uphold any such theory?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- I'm sorry, this is extremely controversial, but I have to say the Muslims were totally committed to expelling -- I won't go into the more graphic ethnically cleansing, but they wanted to expel the Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was their total purpose. They did a very good job of it. They managed to attract international intervention and they managed to win a war that they could not do by themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, my question in French was somewhat different but I believe -- is your answer -- are you a racist or do you support --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question has been clearly answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my question wasn't -- that was not my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was to some extent unclear at least in the English translation because -- I'll ask the witness about it. Mr. Gray, you told us what, in your view, were the aims, whether they were achieved, aims of the Muslims. Do you take this view on the basis of what you saw happening or do you have certain ideas about why people of the Muslim religion would do these kind of things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I have the view from bitter experience. I have seen what the Muslims and the Croats were doing. I have totally contradictory evidence about one specific incident which I am more than happy to relate to you in Court, but the fact is that from my time in the former Yugoslavia, from the 23rd of March until the 1st of December when I left Yugoslavia, my total conviction and understanding is that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the total aim and purpose of the Presidency forces or the Muslim forces, whatever, was to expel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're now repeating what you said before. Let me ask you, when you came to Bosnia, did you have a neutral opinion as to Croats, Serbs, or Muslims or what was your view on these three ethnic groups when arriving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no knowledge of them whatsoever. I had been given a script of the background to the 1991 war but I had -- I had no formed opinion on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That answers my question. Was that different when you left and I'm not talking about what you saw people doing, but your opinion as to the ethnic or religious background that would cause people to do the things you observed them doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was definitely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you explain to me and to the Chamber what? I'm asking you the following, as a matter of fact I will try to make a comparison.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can see that someone who comes from Spain, for example, or a group of people coming from Spain behaving very badly. That does not necessarily mean that Spanish people --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are bad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- are bad or are inclined to do bad things. So you came with a relatively -- I would say neutral or a blank opinion as to the three ethnic groups you mentioned: Croats, Muslims, Serbs, you saw, as you told us, the Muslim forces pursue aims of expelling Serbs, and I do understand that you consider this to be a bad behaviour. What, if any, change this made in your opinion as to Muslim people? I'm asking you to keep in mind what I said about Spanish people misbehaving, I'm not saying that Spanish people misbehave but it's just as an example. Were you just impressed but what they had done or did it change your opinion on what you could expect from Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, in my five and a half months in Sarajevo, I had 11 of my officers wounded. Thankfully, none were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you prefer to have a short break before continuing your answer, because I see that it raises quite some emotion ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll continue. I -- I'm sorry that I have to -- I mean my opinion is based on experience and it was a very, very bitter experience. I was spat at, stoned, shot at, shelled. I had people making -- well, I mean, not nice gestures towards me, and I was there to try and help them. That was all I was there to do and yet that was the response I got. And so yes, that definitely formed an opinion of the people who I was actually trying to help. On the other side, the Serb side, I had nothing but cooperation and assistance. When five of my observers got wounded in one incident by a 122 shell which came from the Croatian side, the Serbs actually assisted -- I mean they went to a Serb hospital in Lukavica barracks and they were assisted there and from there, they were evacuated out to Zagreb. But, I mean, I had nothing but cooperation from the Serb side. I was never threatened, never shot at. It was only -- I mean good cooperation and so if you want to talk about forming an opinion and a feeling for the situation, then that is what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe, since you told us that when arriving, you had a neutral position, when leaving, after what you told us to be bitter experiences, could you describe what your feeling in view of people of Muslim ethnicity or Muslim religion was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I give you some background?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't mind, I would prefer to first hear what your opinion was when you left and of course if you'd like to explain why you formed this opinion, you can do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I was very bitter about the treatment I had received by the Muslims and by the Croats while I was in Sarajevo because of the fact that they tried to kill me on many occasions and that has a certain effect on you. But I go back to the background and say that in 1975 and -- to 1977 I lived in Singapore where there are a large number of Muslims and that's fine and 1985 to 1987 I lived in Malaysia where there are a large number of Muslims. I have no real problem with Muslims. It was to do -- in terms of Sarajevo and Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was more to do with the politics that were happening at that particular time and yes, I was extremely upset at the fact that the UN in general were being targeted by the people that they were actually there to try and help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is two things we need to clarify. You told us about your bitter experience, Colonel, and you told us how -- that you were treated impossibly by the Muslim and the Croat side so my question is as follows: Would you -- do you treat them in the same way, do you put the two of them on the same level? And I'm referring to the treatment that you received from the -- those two sides.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do and -- no, same level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, this will be my very last question: When some questions were put to you about journalists and in particular about a certain commentator, you said, and I'm quoting you from memory, [In English] They got it wrong on several occasions or a certain number of times," [Interpretation] You said something to that effect. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, definitely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Can you tell us exactly what you meant and perhaps give us some specific examples where something said by a journalist was contradicted by the actual situation, the actual facts after an investigation had been carried out, for example?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The journalists came, they were tourists.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object, the questioning in cross-examination related to particular journalists and a particular institution they did not relate to journalists per se, journalists of a particularly high reputation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes and no, because we've spoken about two journalists very frequently, a male journalist and a female journalist and I think that the problem is to know what the witness thinks since one attempted to contradict him in regard to the statements made by both journalists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Not in general whether the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to what we spoke about on Friday, these two particular journalists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to the videos we saw on Friday, you said that very often, journalists committed errors, what did you mean when you said that and could you provide us with examples? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The journalists made assumptions. They assumed that fire was coming from one side or the other and in many cases that we observed and we had observers everywhere on both sides, they got it wrong, and that is why I find the reports that were made by very respected journalists to be quite insulting to the -- the whole effort of the UN in Sarajevo. They got it wrong and we were in a far better position because we had been there for months. They came in for a few days or a few weeks and then they left --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. The answer does nothing to address the concerns I raised earlier in which you ruled in my favour and that is emphasized by the reference to journalists being there for a few days or a few weeks, which seems to be a reference to journalists in a very different category of those that we heard from in the video clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could we please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, after you've responded, I'd like to get the witness back to the subject of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was the idea. I wanted to ask the witness whether what he said also concerns those two persons. That's all I wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You were asked to give examples of where the two journalists from which we saw video footings where they were wrong in what they reported, so not in general but these two, for example, their report on this and this incident was wrong for that and that reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The -- I'll give you one specific incident and that is the so-called shelling of the market. They got it wrong there. I mean I had very experienced officers who went and examined the scene and there was no evidence to actually give any credence to the fact that the market had been shelled or mortared. They found evidence that indicated that a bomb had been placed there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gray, let me interrupt you. You have explained to us that your experts established that it was a bomb and not a shell that landed. So what you say to us is the BBC reporters were wrong there because they ignored that it was a bomb and that they reported that it was a shell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have another example, could you provide us with it? If not, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. There was one incident, it happened at two minutes past 8.00 p.m. On the 13th of July and the -- there had been a number of --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would be grateful if it would be clarified if this relates to either Martin Bell or Kate Adie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, are you giving an example in respect of Mr. Bell or Ms. Adie.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall which one of them, I think it was probably Kate Adie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was BBC.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And what happened was that at two minutes past 8.00 on the 13th of July, there were children, teenagers and we had Canadian soldiers who were throwing sweets, lollies, I don't know whatever you call them, candy, from the top -- the very top of the PTT where we had the observation post established and they were throwing them down to these teenagers down below us. And at two minutes past 8.00 on the 13st of July we had 13 and 16 mortar bombs exploded, they were 82 millimetre, the whole building obviously shook, the mortar bombs landed from a distance of two metres from the PTT building to a distance of 75 metres from the PTT building. I've got the report in my briefcase. We did a crater analysis of those bombs and the actual report that I sent to the headquarters in Zagreb was from the direction of fire that it came from and taking it out to the maximum possible distance of 82 millimetre mortar, it went Muslim, Serb, Muslim, Serb. So we could not tell who actually fired those mortar bombs, we could not tell. We could not in all honesty say who fired them, but the BBC certainly did. They laid the blame clearly on the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you tell us that the reporting was wrong because there was no proper basis for reporting that the 82 millimetre mortar shells had been fired by, I take it, then the BBC reported that it was from the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, before I thank you for your testimony, could you tell us what the consequences of these shots were in terms of the casualties, in terms of the number of dead if there were any?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object, the basis is relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, may I ask you where we are -- we shifted now from wrongly reporting to one of these examples and the consequences, I do not mind but I would like you to be aware that it has hardly anything to do with the cross-examination. But the witness may answer the question. Mr. Gray, do you know what, in terms of human lives the consequences of the shelling were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally carried off the street a teenage boy who had both his legs blown off below the knee. I also held --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object and I wish to say something further in relation to the objection in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, may I ask you to escort the witness for one second out of the courtroom. Mr. Gray.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we have visitors in the public gallery, we first would have to ask them to leave the public gallery since we cannot shield that off when we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the public gallery open again? It should be certain that those who were following the proceedings are in the position to come to the public gallery again. Yes. Mr. Gray, you have been asked a question about casualties on an occasion where soldiers had been giving sweets to -- well, children, teenagers. You have been asked about the casualties and we noticed that this, of course, might cause you to, going back to that time, to undergo emotional moments again. In your absence, one of the aspects we have discussed is whether there's any disagreement between the parties as to whether kids had been killed at that occasion. The parties do not disagree on that so therefore, also in order to save you to undergo again these emotions, you don't have to answer that question unless you would say it's totally wrong what you say, kids were not killed, but I take it that you are telling us that how you personally experienced what happened to these kids. We are not asking you to go any further because we are aware of what that could mean to you and since the parties do not disagree, Court will assume that at that occasion, young people were killed, since the parties do not disagree. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've finished with this answer. I just wanted to thank the witness for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He's not finished today, there might be some questions for you both from the Bench and from the Prosecution but we'll first have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I just make one comment about that particular incident? I mean I think the Defence counsel were talking about misreporting by the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was reported very clearly as being an attack by the Serbs. We were there. We did the investigation, and we couldn't determine because of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you told us that. You said it was Serb, Muslim, Serb, Muslim, so you could not establish whereas the report did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have not seen the report but we do understand your testimony to be that they gave information --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before we break, the witness did mention that he had a report in relation to this incident. I don't know that I've seen that report perhaps I could have a look at it over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there -- did you bring any report with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't bring that particular report with me, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it your report to Zagreb that you indicated. But you haven't brought it with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, a report was made to Zagreb about the actual incident and it was then passed on to the UN headquarters in New York but I -- I think I probably got it on a computer disc which the Defence have, I mean I've given them five computer discs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's not something you could retrieve immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just to clarify that, Mr. President, five computer discs, we've seen one and perhaps the number of videos could be clarified because I still haven't been able to find on the four video discs two of the passages given to us by the Defence if we could just clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many discs did you give to the Defence? You said five.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two CDs, one of which has got -- because all of the work was done on WordPerfect 5.1 at the time in 1992, okay. There is one CD which has got actual WordPerfect on it and then there is another CD which has got a copy of the five computer discs that -- three and a half floppy discs that I've given to them as well and I believe I actually gave them five videotapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me just -- first you said one CD with all the WordPerfect 5.1 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- files. Yes, that's what we used in these times, isn't it? Then you said five floppy discs transferred into another CD. What would be on that other CD? Would that be the same or different, would it be text would it be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is all text and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Text created by yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's all from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And there is one of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would allow me just to interrupt you. Is that text on the second CD and the first one being with WordPerfect 5.1 files, that second CD would that be different text from the first one you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it will be and there is one extra --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you tell us in what format, what under what software these texts are created.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are all in WordPerfect 5.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So on both CDs, we would find WordPerfect 5.1 files but with a different content.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the first CD has got the actual programme file for WordPerfect 5.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the second one --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the second one has got four of the five discs actually recorded on to it, transferred on to it because I wanted to make sure that there were two copies and there is one, a further fifth disc which is not on the CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I will repeat, one CD with the WordPerfect 5.1 programme software, another CD on which is transferred the content of four floppy discs containing WordPerfect 5.1 files, and a fifth floppy disc not being transferred on that CD-ROM but still available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then about videotapes, how many did you provide to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall that I provided five videotapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, do you still have copies of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No I just brought them with me and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not four, five.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe there were five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I invite the parties to discuss during the break what is -- what has been disclosed, what has not been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President. I actually raised that with the Defence this morning. I'm assured that they only received four. I would be grateful if we could have access to those four videotapes as soon as possible when they're no longer needed in Court so that we can make copies of them in order for us to discover if they are on those tapes or not. That's an issue we'll have to deal with when it's witness leaves but at least if we can have access to copy them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes I think that would be a fair request and I see the Defence is nodding yes, so the Chamber expects the parties to cooperate in this respect. Mr. Gray, we'll not adjourn until 11.00, but until five minutes past 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we discussed the matter of exhibits with the Prosecution during the break. What we can say here that when the witness gave us four floppy discs, that is true, but the information that we received from him at the time was that these floppy discs were taken over to CDs and we were able to open these floppy -- we were not able to open these floppy discs perhaps because of the programme or perhaps because there was something else there. We do not know. But at any rate, those floppy discs that we still have them and they are of course at the disposal of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Presumably still in the hands of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, I think the Defence is saying they've got them and we weren't told about them before today. We were given four videos and one CD. We were told the Defence couldn't open the CD. We managed to open it and we gave the Defence copies of all of the documents that we were able to obtain from the CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just first check whether I rightly understood the observations by Mr. Piletta-Zanin. It's not entirely clear to me, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I'm just looking to the English transcript at this moment. You said that you received four floppy discs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four or five, four or five. We need to check it because I cannot really tell you off the cuff how many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are taken over to a CD, did you do that or did the witness provide you with the CD?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the CD is one of the two that we just talked about. At the time we understood that all of the material had been copied to those CDs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The case and that therefore, the one who is in possession of the fifth floppy disc -- yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution was only given one CD. It seems the Defence is saying they received from the witness two CDs and five floppy discs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the CDs as the witness explained to us is just WordPerfect 5.1 which is a programme which is not generally installed on computers anymore as it was in 1992 so one is just the programme software and the other CD is assumed to contain the content of the four floppy discs but not of the fifth and so the most important thing now is to find out where is the fifth floppy disc?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall check. Perhaps there are, indeed, five and we shall check whether this last one, whether -- we are not sure whether there are four or five floppy discs and whether perhaps they are here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Did not take the effort to provide the fifth floppy disc if you have it because you expected it to be on the second CD-ROM.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed that was the information that we believe to have received, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the second issue is about the videotapes. Is there any comparison as to what the Defence thinks it has and what the Prosecution thinks it has?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, from what we know, on the tapes that we saw in full or in part, there is frequent repetition. There are things which are repeated, and what we have done was put -- place all these tapes to the Prosecution, and we shall do it in the afternoon so they can go through all of them and check them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Perhaps not yet settled but at least this issue being proceeded we could then continue with the examination of the witness. Mr. Ierace, since you asked to cross-examine the witness on those issues that have come up for the first time in the re-examination, perhaps it would be proper to start with that and then hear whether there are any questions from the Bench and then the parties then get an opportunity to respond to -- if necessary, to put additional questions on those issues raised by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just while the witness is being brought in, might I suggest a procedure in relation to the tendering of the videotapes? If -- I understand that one of Mr. Gray's original videotapes has already been tendered. If the other one is formally tendered, then after the Prosecution has made copies, they could supplant the tendered ones which could then be returned to Mr. Gray by mail or however is convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think at least for the Defence we tendered the original of a tape but we are not quite sure. Perhaps the Prosecution didn't quite understand us because what we said was that we had made a selection and presented -- that we produced it on one tape with eight or nine different fragments which is not the original provided by Mr. Gray. We simply copied it to a different tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that this -- that you intend to tender this videotape containing those elements that you thought relevant from the tapes provided to you by Mr. Gray.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think what's happened is that the original Gray tape with the brown Mercedes clip has been tendered. We have made a tape with just that clip so already, that could replace the full videotape that Madam Registrar presently has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think the important thing is that we are able to retain the two original BBC tapes until such time as they are copied and then they can be returned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it -- but that's apart from tendering these tapes, that they should be copied so that we have a copy of the full Gray tapes available for consultation for the parties and that you are going to tender the extracts thought to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I also ask you, the full version of the -- what I would call the night attack on the Presidency parliamentary building, is that already prepared?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the best copy that we've been able to make of the relevant part of that segment is still of a very poor quality, in particular, there are some horizontal lines which appear on the copy and which do not appear on the original which is quite confusing when one's looking at the tracer fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would therefore respectfully suggest that you look at the relevant part of that clip on the original Gray tape. We have prepared a full transcript of that part of the clip; in other words, the shooting of the parliamentary building and I might add while I'm on my feet, over the weekend we've already prepared a translation of the brown Mercedes clip, all of that clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem, Mr. President, is to know what will be finally be tendered. If it is only the night attack then one cannot tender obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I take it that a -- perhaps in the near future a better copy of that segment can be made but at least we'd like to see in this court at this moment the -- that part of the original. Could it be identified for the technical booth if it could be played that we know where to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think we've made some identification of that, I used the word "translation" of the brown Mercedes clip, translation should have been transcription.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes this transcript is then ready to be translated by the interpreters if necessary. Mr. Ierace, in order to avoid a lot of confusion and -- could you tell us what subjects you consider to be appropriate to address in a further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The issue of the primaries, that is if I can refer to it in that shorthand fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And secondly the witness has said for the first time that in relation to the -- what we might call the French convoy, the convoy had been sitting at Lukavica barracks over night and was due to come into Sarajevo at 10.00 a.m. and that is -- that stands contradicted by Kate Adie who referred to the French convoy coming in at dusk the night before so I wish to question him about that. Mr. President, in relation to the events of the 13th of July, naturally the Prosecution will seek to obtain from the BBC a copy of their report in relation to that incident. There are some questions I could ask of the witness as to how the teenagers came to be there, I can tell you what I understand to be the situation. That could turn out to be relevant to the contents of the BBC clip. Of course by the time we get that, Mr. Gray will no longer be here. The questions I would put to him on that issue are drawn from General MacKenzie's book so an alternative may be if we get the BBC report, we then tender that with General MacKenzie's account as taken from his book. If you like, Mr. President, I can tell you in summary form what that account is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I've got one problem if you would do so, that is, that if at a later stage the witness for whatever reason would be recalled, that it's on the public transcript what we --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We can do it in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I heard that the Prosecution intended to do two things. First, concerning the incident of the humanitarian convoy, the contradiction between the daybreak and the position of the witness was treated during the cross-examination by Mr. Ierace and I -- if I remember that the witness has said something, I'm not quoting, but I think that that is what he said and that he said clearly when that was. That is quite clear. As for the PTT incident, we, at the Defence, appreciate in particular, that is, we bore in mind the personality of this witness. We saw him. To go back to that would really be achieving again, the same effect and again the Defence would like to spare this witness any further distress, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The witness testified, as far as I can see: "Okay, I actually arranged for a cease-fire with the warring parties. You can see from the video pictures I mean it was an -- an arranged for a specific time for that convoy to actually come through. You can see from the pictures that it was broad daylight and the convoy was deliberately targeted, I mean it was clearly identifiable," so the witness says that it appears from the video does this broad daylight so there seems there is a possible contradiction and I think it could be clarified in one or two questions so that would not be something we -- the Chamber would not allow. And then as far as the second issue is concerned, are we in --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn it to private session so will that Mr. Ierace can explain what -- because the if the parties agree on how the teenagers got there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session, again. So could you tell us whether you know anything specific about why these youngsters were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a beautiful sunny day in July, obviously, and the youngsters were -- I mean they were teenagers between 16 and 18, I would say. The Canadian troops who were actually on top of the fifth floor of the PTT -- I mean there was no shelling, there was no -- no war activity actually happening at the time and that's why it was unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It may assist I think the witness may have misunderstood the question not so much why they were on the ground outside the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mr. Gray, were they accidentally gathered together there or was this group constituted in one way or another of which you have any knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were accidentally there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then confront you with what General MacKenzie writes in a book that is that these youngsters were of a group that was exchanged Serbians against -- let me just read it to you, "What made matters worse was that most of the teenagers had come to the PTT in a population exchange organised earlier in the day by Richard Gray. He had delivered some Serbs to Lukavica in exchange had brought back a load of people including the teenagers who wished to return to downtown Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's true. So they were not accidentally there but they were there as a result of an exchange of population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I had brought them back earlier on in the day so I mean there was a time lapse between me bringing them back and them actually being at the PTT.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At what time did you -- how long did they stay there before the shells fell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had brought them back earlier on several hours beforehand but I -- one of the young women who was actually killed, I physically recognised her clothing, I mean I recognised her, I mean she was quite badly -- I mean she was killed. But I mean this happened at 8.00 at night and the exchange that took place happened earlier on in the day and maybe mid-day, very early afternoon. I mean maybe 1.00 in the afternoon. But I mean that happened -- a number of hours before this actually happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Gray. Mr. Ierace has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Further cross-examination by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gray, in relation to the use of primaries when firing mortars, is it your understanding that the purpose of the primary is to ignite the charges however many there may be, in the tube?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are actually around the tail fin of the actual mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And have you ever fired a mortar on its primary alone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts did you do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that in Waiouru in New Zealand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please spell that for the benefit of the transcribers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's W-a-i-o-u-r-u.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it explained to you that a mortar should only be fired on its primary in an emergency?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A primary -- I mean you only fire a mortar on primary when you are under immediate attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. And correct me if I am wrong, that's because they are not nearly so accurate when fired just on the primary and there is a degree, an element or degree of danger when firing on the primary?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are more accurate when they are on primary. They have a shorter distance in terms of the impact but they are actually more accurate because the more charges you use with a mortar, the further it goes, the higher it goes, the less accurate it is at the other end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to suggest to you that your understanding is quite incorrect. Specifically when a mortar is fired on its primary it is far less accurate than if it is fired with charges.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell General MacKenzie what you have told us in court in relation to the primaries; in other words, that you heard two sounds that you concluded were primaries seconds before the two mortars landed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that immediately after, I mean as I told you in the Court on Friday, I told him immediately after the meeting, I went back and I made a verbal report to him and then I made a written report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I suppose at the time, you appreciated how important that information was because in your mind it was conclusive proof that it had been -- the mortars had been fired --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have the impression that we are moving to another subject which has been dealt with extensively, that of the relationship between the witness and General MacKenzie after this incident and we're no longer discussing the technique involved in primaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Is not -- has not come up I think new in cross-examination -- in re-examination, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this relates specifically to the primaries whether he told General MacKenzie that he had heard the primaries --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That answer has been given if I'm correct, the witness said "I believe I did".

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. And this question, Mr. President, goes to whether he indeed is sure that he would have because of its importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then the last question on the issue you may put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As you please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suppose at the time you appreciated the importance of your observation because, in your mind, it established that the mortars had been fired from the Presidency side of the confrontation lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were -- excuse me, we were running a sweepstake on this particular event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gray you told us about the sweepstake. Now, you also, this morning, were asked some questions about the humanitarian aid convoy operated by French troops that were shot at when it arrived at Sarajevo and you said this morning, "The convoy had been sitting at Lukavica barracks overnight and was due to come in at 10.00 a.m.," is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember -- excuse me, Mr. President, that Kate Adie on the voiceover for this incident referred to the French convoy being shot at as it approached at dusk the day before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think her words were, "These men were part of a routine UN convoy from Belgrade, 35 vehicles nearing Sarajevo airport at dusk yesterday." Mr. Gray, I think you've told us you weren't there, you didn't see the convoy approach. Do you dispute that it, in fact, arrived at dusk and not at 10.00 a.m. in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness has repeated, on several occasions, his answer to this question. He's provided a clear answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know where Mr. Piletta-Zanin gets that from, since the time issue only arose this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to "broad daylight," Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you dispute that the convoy was shot at as it arrived at dusk?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that it arrived at 10.00 a.m.; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that it arrived in broad daylight and it was not at dusk. You can have it. I mean look at the video.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gray, do you know -- I withdraw that. What was your information as to when, that is, what time of day, the convoy was shot at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like the clip on the brown Mercedes be shown to the witness, but only one of the images, not the complete clip. I think that the technical booth knows that. Okay. That's the picture. Mr. Gray, you told us that to the right-hand side was the building of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Well, do you know which building is the one that you can see behind the trees at the right-hand side? It's -- not yellow but ...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two buildings there is the Presidency building and -- which is -- it's actually shielded by the vehicles you can see on the right-hand side of the screen and then there is another building where I had my -- the Papa headquarters was actually based. I know because I was in that building and I actually helped to put the antenna up on the actual roof of that building. But the Presidency building is the one to the right-hand side and it's shielded basically by the vehicles which are moving away from where the mortar attack happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: In fact, we can't see the Presidency building.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't. You can't see it. You can't actually see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gray. You are an experienced artillery officer, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have experience with mortars, I have worked with artillery many times but I mean I am -- well, I was an infantry officer but I have done courses with both artillery and with mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Well, if, in theory, I'm talking in theory, if you are in front of a building used by snipers, how can you get rid of the snipers? Which weapon would you use in that case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would use any weapon that was at my disposal in order to actually get rid of them, whether it be by tank fire, whether it would be by small arms fire. I wouldn't try to use mortars because it doesn't really work that well because mortars come directly down. I would use artillery but probably not mortars, but I mean I would use anything at my disposal to actually get rid of the sniper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: You mentioned the other day that there were two agreements, big ones, agreements, and you said the following, "The second agreement was not honoured by the UN."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Could you elaborate a little bit on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When General MacKenzie withdrew from -- by I mean he withdrew himself from Sarajevo, there was a vacuum created and we had a French chief of staff, Colonel d'Avout, a very nice man but he was a chief of staff not a commander so we had this vacuum and so nothing was happening, the war was going on but we had the airport agreement and then we had the agreement for the concentration of weapons and I decided that something had to be done so I went out and I concluded in August and September a second agreement for the concentration of all heavy weapons and that was concluded in August and September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gray. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has one or more questions for you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to thank you for the effort you have made and for the information that you have provided us with. There are a few questions that I would like to ask you and in fact it's a matter of verifying certain matters. If I have understood you correctly, my first question has to do with the shelling of the building where you and some UN members were present, where you were shelled at. If I have understood you correctly, you said that you had asked for an explanation from the commander or deputy commander on the Serb side who was located in Nedzarici. You asked him why he had shelled the building and he replied that that building was close to the confrontation line. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building was on the confrontation line, it was actually part of the front line. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] That's right. That's right, exactly. So in responses to the questions put to you, you said that there were forces that gathered from this building in order to prepare possible attacks but if I've understood you correctly, if I have understood the answer of the commander of the Serbian forces who told you that this building was part of the confrontation line, he wasn't speaking about the preparation of troops or he wasn't speaking on the basis of knowledge of troops getting ready because you lived in that building and you yourself were able to see these troops gathering. Did the Serb commander know about what was being prepared in this building?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. As I explained, I think, on Friday, the -- this -- these buildings, I mean, were like this and they formed -- it was a -- what in military terms we call a forming-up place, I mean this is where the troops actually formed behind the buildings and they actually attacked Nedzarici from behind these buildings.
